name: Public Speaking and Presenting
objectives: For a topic you know well, write down your audience, your goal for them and your one big idea, with the big idea in one sentence
For a 2-minute talk, outline a hook, three key points with examples and a close with one call to action, on one page of short notes
For your talk, decide whether you need slides and make no more than three simple ones if you do, with one idea per slide and every fact checked
Before giving the talk, practise out loud with a timer and use breathing to manage nerves, finishing in 2 minutes or less
While speaking, use your voice, eye contact and posture to sound and look confident, fixing at least one thing you noticed on your recording
After a talk, answer questions calmly, including ones you cannot answer, repeating each question and ending with your big idea

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Planning a short talk: audience, goal and one big idea
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write down your audience, your goal and your one big idea for a short talk.
This lesson builds toward: For a topic you know well, you will write down your audience, your goal for them and your one big idea, with the big idea in one sentence.
Before you write a single word, answer three questions. Who is listening? What do I want them to do, think or feel afterward? What is the one big idea I want them to remember?
The same topic changes with the audience. Talking about your nonprofit's food pantry to donors, you might focus on results and what their money does. To new volunteers, you would focus on what a shift looks like. To a youth team, a coach talking about discipline would use their own games as examples.
Write your big idea as one sentence a 12-year-old could repeat: "Showing up early every day is what wins close games." or "Our app saves small shops two hours a week." Everything in your talk should support that sentence. If something does not, cut it.
Step by step:
- Write who is listening and what they care about.
- Write what you want them to do, think or feel after.
- Write your one big idea in one simple sentence.
- Check: does each thing you plan to say support the big idea?
Words to know:
- Audience: the people listening to your talk.
- Big idea: the one main message you want people to remember.
Try it now: Pick a topic you know well for your 2-minute talk. Write your audience, your goal for them and your one big idea in one sentence.
You can now plan a talk by choosing your audience, your goal and one big idea.

check.q: Why think about your audience before writing a talk?
options: So you can use bigger words
So the talk fits what they need and care about
So you can speak longer
So you can skip practice
check.why: Knowing the audience helps you choose what matters to them.

check.q: You are speaking to young players about joining your club. What would you make your big idea?
options: A full history of the club since it began
A list of every rule
Why joining the club will help them grow and have fun
Your own win record
check.why: The big idea should be the one message this audience needs to remember.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Structure: hook, three points, close
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Outline a 2-minute talk with a hook, three key points and a clear close.
This lesson builds toward: For a 2-minute talk, you will outline a hook, three key points with examples and a close with one call to action, on one page of short notes.
A simple structure helps your listeners follow you and helps you remember what comes next. Use: hook, three points, close.
The hook grabs attention in the first 15 seconds: a short story, a surprising fact, or a question. "Last season we lost four games by one point." Then give three key points. Three is easy to remember. Back each with an example or a number. Then close: repeat your big idea and tell people what to do next. "Come early this week. I will be there at 6." or "Sign up for one shift by Friday."
For a 2-minute talk, that is roughly 15 seconds for the hook, 30 seconds per point and 15 seconds for the close. Write the outline as short notes, not a full script, so you sound natural.
Step by step:
- Write a hook: story, surprising fact or question.
- Write three key points, each with one example or number.
- Write a close: repeat the big idea and ask for one action.
- Time it: about 15 s hook, 30 s per point, 15 s close.
Words to know:
- Hook: an opening that grabs attention.
- Call to action: telling the audience the one thing to do next.
- Outline: a short list of the parts of your talk, in order.
Try it now: Write the outline for your 2-minute talk: one hook, three points with an example each, and a close with one call to action. Keep it to short notes on one page or one phone note.
You can now outline a short talk with a hook, three key points and a close with a call to action.

check.q: What is the job of a hook?
options: To grab attention in the first few seconds
To end the talk
To list your three points
To thank the audience
check.why: A hook gets people listening right away.

check.q: Your outline has seven key points for a 2-minute talk. What would you do?
options: Talk faster to fit them in
Add more slides
Keep them all and skip the close
Choose the three most important points
check.why: Three points fit the time and are easy to remember.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Simple slides that help, not hurt
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Make simple slides, or decide you do not need any.
This lesson builds toward: For your talk, you will decide whether you need slides and make no more than three simple ones if you do, with one idea per slide and every fact checked.
Slides should help the audience, not hold your script. Many great short talks use no slides at all. Use them when a picture, a chart or a few key words make your point clearer.
Rules that work: one idea per slide; a short title; at most a few words or one picture; big text that people at the back can read; high contrast, like dark text on a light background. Never read your slides out loud word for word; the audience can read faster than you talk.
Free tools such as Google Slides, Microsoft PowerPoint for the web and Canva let you make slides in a browser. An AI assistant can suggest slide titles from your outline, but cut its text down hard and check every fact and number it gives you.
Step by step:
- Ask: does a slide make this point clearer? If not, skip it.
- One idea per slide with a short title.
- Use a few words or one picture.
- Make the text big with strong contrast.
- Practise without reading the slides out loud.
Words to know:
- Slide deck: a set of slides for a talk.
- Contrast: how much the text stands out from the background.
Try it now: Decide whether your 2-minute talk needs slides. If yes, make no more than three in a free tool, one idea each. If no, write one sentence about why the talk works without them.
You can now make simple, readable slides or decide confidently to speak without them.

check.q: When does a slide help a talk?
options: When it holds your whole script
When a picture, chart or few words make a point clearer
When you have nothing to say
Always, on every sentence
check.why: Slides help only when they make a point clearer.

check.q: An AI assistant gives you a slide packed with 80 words. What would you do?
options: Read it word for word
Make the text smaller
Add more words
Cut it to a short title and a few words, and check the facts
check.why: Simple slides with checked facts help; walls of text hurt.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Practice and nerves
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Practise a talk out loud and use simple tools to manage nerves.
This lesson builds toward: Before giving the talk, you will practise out loud with a timer and use breathing to manage nerves, finishing in 2 minutes or less.
Nerves are normal, even for professional speakers and athletes before a big game. A fast heart and shaky hands are your body getting ready. You do not need to get rid of nerves; you need to use them.
Practice is the best cure. Say the talk out loud at least three times, standing up, with a timer. Then record it on your phone and watch it back. Then try it in front of one friend, family member, coach or coworker. Each round, it gets easier.
On the day: breathe slowly (in for 4, out for 6) before you start; hold your notes or rest your hands; find a friendly face in the room; and remember the audience wants you to do well. If you lose your place, pause, look at your notes and carry on. A pause feels long to you but short to them.
Step by step:
- Say the talk out loud three times, standing, with a timer.
- Record it on your phone and watch it back.
- Practise once in front of one person and ask for one tip.
- Before you start: breathe in for 4, out for 6.
- If you lose your place: pause, check notes, carry on.
Words to know:
- Rehearse: practise a talk out loud before giving it.
- Nerves: the nervous feeling before something important; normal and useful.
Try it now: Stand up and say your 2-minute talk out loud three times with a timer. Note how long each run takes and cut anything that pushes you past 2 minutes.
You can now rehearse a talk out loud, time it, and use breathing and pauses to manage nerves.

check.q: What does it mean when your heart beats fast before a talk?
options: Your body is getting ready, which is normal
You should cancel the talk
You are not prepared
You are sick
check.why: Nerves are a normal sign your body is getting ready.

check.q: Your practice run takes 3 minutes, but you have 2. What would you do?
options: Speak much faster
Skip the close on the day
Cut parts that do not support your big idea and time it again
Ask for more time on the day
check.why: Cutting extra parts keeps the talk on time and focused.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Voice and body language
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use your voice, eyes and body to sound and look confident.
This lesson builds toward: While speaking, you will use your voice, eye contact and posture to sound and look confident, fixing at least one thing you noticed on your recording.
How you say it matters as much as what you say. Speak a little slower and a little louder than in normal conversation. Pause after important points to let them land. Change your tone so you do not sound flat, and cut filler words such as "um" and "like" by pausing instead.
Stand tall with your feet about shoulder-width apart and your weight even. Keep your hands relaxed at your sides or use them for natural gestures; avoid crossing your arms or keeping hands in your pockets. Look at real people, one at a time, for a sentence or two each. In a video call, look at the camera, not at your own face on the screen.
Different cultures read eye contact and gestures differently, so watch your audience and adjust. The goal is to look calm, open and interested in them.
Step by step:
- Speak a little slower and louder than normal.
- Pause after important points.
- Replace "um" with a short pause.
- Stand tall, feet shoulder-width apart, hands relaxed.
- Look at one person for a sentence, then another.
- On video, look at the camera.
Words to know:
- Body language: what your posture, face, hands and eyes say without words.
- Filler words: sounds like "um", "uh" and "like" that fill silence.
Try it now: Record 30 seconds of your talk on your phone. Watch it with the sound off: check posture, hands and eyes. Then listen with your eyes closed: count the "um"s and notice your speed. Pick one thing to fix.
You can now use your voice, posture, hands and eye contact to come across as calm and confident.

options: A key word in your big idea
A word like "um" or "like" that fills a pause
A word on a slide
The last word of your talk
check.why: Filler words fill silence; a short pause works better.

check.q: Watching your recording, you see yourself looking at the floor. What would you do?
options: Look at one person for a sentence, then another
Close your eyes while you speak
Read your notes the whole time
Look only at the ceiling
check.why: Eye contact with one person at a time looks confident.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Handling questions
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Answer questions after a talk calmly and clearly, including ones you cannot answer.
This lesson builds toward: After a talk, you will answer questions calmly, including ones you cannot answer, repeating each question and ending with your big idea.
Questions mean people were listening. Prepare by writing the three questions you are most likely to get and a short answer for each.
When someone asks: listen to the whole question, thank them, and repeat or rephrase it so everyone hears it. Answer briefly, in 30 seconds or less if you can, and then check: "Does that answer your question?" If you do not know, say so honestly: "I don't know, but I will find out and get back to you by Friday." Then do it. Never make something up.
For a hostile or off-topic question, stay calm and polite: "That's a fair concern. Let's talk after so we can give it proper time." A reporter or a sponsor may ask tricky questions too; bridge back to your big idea: "What I can tell you is...". Finish the question time with your close again so your big idea is the last thing people hear.
Step by step:
- Before: write three likely questions and short answers.
- Listen to the whole question.
- Thank them and repeat it for everyone.
- Answer briefly, then check it answered them.
- Don't know? Say so and promise to follow up.
- End by repeating your close.
Words to know:
- Q&A: short for questions and answers: the time after a talk for questions.
- Bridge: a phrase that moves a tricky answer back to your main message.
Try it now: Final task: record your 2-minute talk on your phone. Then have a friend ask you two questions (or ask yourself two) and record your answers. Watch it back, note one strength and one fix, and record the talk once more.
You can now deliver a short talk and handle questions calmly, including ones you cannot answer yet.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Big idea The talk has no clear main message. One big idea a listener could repeat in one sentence. The big idea fits the audience and their needs. Structure Missing a hook, a point or a close. A hook, three key points with examples and a close with one call to action. The close repeats the big idea and the call to action is specific. Time Over 2 minutes, or clearly not practised. Finishes in 2 minutes or less, from notes, not a script. Sounds natural and calm from start to finish. Voice and body Hard to hear, many filler words, or no eye contact. Clear voice, steady pace, good posture and eye contact with the camera. The second recording shows the fix chosen after watching the first. Answering questions Made up answers or got defensive. Repeated each question and answered calmly, or promised to follow up. Bridged back to the big idea at the end. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a bridge in answering questions?
options: A slide that links two points
A pause before your talk
A phrase that takes you from the question back to your main message
A way to avoid every question
check.why: A bridge like "What I can tell you is..." brings you back to your message.

check.q: Someone asks a question you cannot answer. What would you say?
options: Make up an answer
Ignore the question
Tell them it is a bad question
"I don't know, but I'll find out and get back to you by Friday."
check.why: Honesty plus a set follow-up day keeps trust.
